He does not want a situation — For instance, I will mention a name— I know Colleagues whose children chose particular schools and the Hon Minister ensured that nobody manipulated and ensured that they got their schools of choice. This, the Hon Minister for Education has done and done so confidently, efficiently and to the satisfaction of Members. So, he should not misquote me. Mr Speaker: Hon Member, enough is enough. Mr Afenyo-Markin: Indeed, Mr Speaker. Dr Ato-Forson: Mr Speaker, the issue before us is a matter of public concern. It calls for total unity of this House in addressing the concerns of our constituents. No one has politicised the issue before us. Can you imagine that from the Minister’s Statement, the computer school placement was released on Tuesday, 28th November? Let us pay attention to this date. Clearly, the date it was released cannot be counted as if every single person may have been able to access and be aware where they have been placed. Mr Speaker, subsequently, the next day, 29th November, was a Wednesday. Thursday was 30th November. Friday was Farmers Day. Saturday, Sunday, and today is Monday, the day they are supposed to travel. This means that they had only two working days to prepare, buy the things that have been advertised in the prospectus and go to school. 151 4th December, 2023 152 Statements Mr Speaker, those of us from rural Ghana are aware that often, when students write examination of this nature, they travel to sometimes live with their relatives in certain parts of the country. It is only after the results have been released that they come back home. Some may have not been back since then, and that is a fact. Mr Speaker, aside that, I have seen the prospectus, and my Colleagues have taken us through the prospectus. One will need over GH₵7000. We recognise that they are not paying tuition fees. One would need GH₵5,000 to GH₵8,000, depending on what one is buying. It will be wrong for us in this Chamber to assume that because we can afford GH₵5,000 easily, everybody out there can afford GH₵5,000 in days. We all know the state of the economy. Even us, we are among only about 0.1 per cent of the population. So, if one is to take the population of 35 million, MPs here are among the privileged 0.1 per cent. That is approximately 3500 people. So, if they can afford it, it does not mean their constituents can afford it in days. Mr Speaker, the matter raised by the Ranking Member is for the Minister responsible for Education to consider extending the date — that is not politicisation and that cannot be politicisation — so that our constituents, who are lucky enough that they have been placed, would be able to organise themselves and then go to school. As a Member of Parliament, I have received calls, text messages and WhatsApp messages from my constituents, asking for help, and I

or a particular year of a particular Government. We are looking at the bigger picture; hence we cannot deal with this matter on the Floor of the House. So, probably, I was thinking that Mr Speaker, in your wisdom, would do some referral, that the Committee on Education should engage the Hon Minister. There, they can do a detailed assessment of the subject matter. But now that Mr Speaker has given the directive that the Hon Minister should come with a Statement, I think we should all go by that. We would urge the Hon Minister to do it. Nobody is saying that his Ministry is under judgement. We are looking at an absolute concern related to the educational sector and we are not relating it to any Government or— Mr Speaker, I think we will go by your directive, and allow the Hon Minister to come to the Floor of this House and present a Statement to this effect. 83 6th December, 2023 84 Statements Mr Speaker: Hon Members, I will allow the Hon Minister to come with a Statement on this matter and put his perspectives before the House for us to look at. Based on that, if there is the need for us to refer the matter to the subject matter Committee to sit with other stakeholders for us to review the whole educational sector, then we will do so. I think that is the proper thing to do. This is because, as you know, Statements should not be reduced to debates, they are just comments to be made. So, we would like that to be done. Hon Minister, as you come, it will be very good if you have some data that could assist the House because you are in charge of the sector. You may not make general statements like the ordinary Hon Members, so come with some data on how things are being turned around and we would all look at whether to go with the steps that are being taken now or introduce new initiatives to change things. More importantly, if you could come up with a Statement to show how the issue of values, ethics, integrity and honesty—those issues that have been raised—are being addressed, it will be important to all of us. Also, you may look at how relevant the education is now to the situation in our country. How is it helping us to solve the challenges that we face as a nation? With this, Hon Members, we have come to the end of Statements. We have other things that we have to move on to and I am to receive some important guests, so I will take a few things and hand over to the Hon First Deputy Speaker. Hon Members will recall that a few days ago, I stopped the Hon Member for Bawku Central, Mr Mahama Ayariga, from laying a Petition. I think the time is now for him to do so. Then, we will move to some other Papers to be laid, which my attention has now been

education. It is emphatic that basic education should be compulsory for every child of school going age. However, the focus on the SHS level at the expense of the basic level in recent times, motivated by the Free SHS policy has further exacerbated the deterioration of quality education in the country. Mr Speaker, the perceived prevailing climate of fear and intimidation has restricted the ability of school administrators to voice out their concerns regarding the declining quality of education. Many headteachers and principals feel constrained and unable to express their grievances openly for fear of losing their jobs. Consequently, the lack of constructive dialogue and effective problem-solving within the educational system has untold negative repercussions on quality education in the country. Mr Speaker, Parent-Teacher Associa- tions (PTAs) hitherto, played a crucial role in supporting Government in the running of schools. PTAs have been instrumental in providing school needs, including infrastructure, vehicles, motivation of staff and other administrative needs of schools. However, due to perceived political expedience by Government, schools have been cautioned not to allow parents to contribute towards school development. It is sad to note that some heads were reprimanded for asking parents to pay PTA levies. The decision to stop parents from contributing towards their children’s education has run down some schools drastically because PTAs remained the backbone of the development of some schools. Mr Speaker, Ghana’s international reputation in the field of education has suffered a setback due to the pervasive decline in standards, diminishing the country’s credibility and competitive- ness on the global stage. According to the 2018 World Development report, Ghana has been ranked second to last in education globally. This has placed Ghana among the worse countries on education worldwide, an alarming cause to worry about. Besides, Ghana’s educational system risks producing half-baked graduates whose performance is likely to affect us in diverse forms, socially, economically, culturally, health-wise and even in sustainable development. In addition, our hope of transforming Ghana into an industrial nation is likely to suffer setbacks as a result of the poor quality of education if care is not taken. 45 6th December, 2023 46 Statements Mr Speaker, urgent measures must be implemented to address the critical issues plaguing the Ghanaian educational system. Immediate attention should be directed towards revitalising the neglected basic education level, including the provision of essential resources and infrastructure, such as teachers, school buildings, furniture, teaching and learning materials, among others. Mr Speaker, Government, as a matter of urgency, must free the PTAs to do their work. Empowerment of PTAs must be facilitated to enable their active participation and support in the educational sector. It is a fact that Government alone cannot shoulder the burden of education, hence a collaborative approach between the Government and PTA is more sustainable and the way to go. Mr Speaker, it is imperative for Government to prioritise the educational sector by fulfilling its commitments and allocating sufficient resources to ensure the effective functioning of educational institutions. Revising the existing promotion and demotion policies within the educational system could foster a more conducive environment
